gaborone: Gaborone lies between Kgale Hill and Oodi Hill, near the confluence of the Notwane and Segoditshane rivers, in the south-eastern corner of Botswana and within 15 kilometres of the South African border. It stands at an elevation of 1,010 metres and has a hot semi-arid climate. Several neighbouring towns, among them Mogoditshane, Mochudi and Tlokweng across the river, are largely commuter towns for the city.

There have been inhabitants along the Notwane River for centuries. Around 1880 the Tlokwa left the Magaliesberg ranges to settle the area and called the settlement Moshaweng. The word Gaborone is said to mean "it does not fit badly" or "it is not unbecoming". Early European colonizers called the place Gaberones, a shortening of "Gaborone's Village", after Chief Gaborone of the Tlokwa, whose home village, now called Tlokweng, lay across the river from the Government Camp, the colonial government's headquarters. The nickname GC comes from Government Camp.

In 1890 Cecil John Rhodes picked Gaberones to house a colonial fort, where he planned the Jameson Raid. In the mid-1960s, when the Bechuanaland Protectorate became an independent nation, the city was planned as its capital. It was chosen because it was not affiliated with any specific indigenous group and was close to fresh water. The name changed from Gaberones to Gaborone in 1969. The city grew very fast, which has caused problems of housing and illegal settlement, and it dealt with conflicts spilling over from Zimbabwe and South Africa in the 1980s.

Gaborone is the capital and largest city of Botswana, with 246,325 inhabitants at the 2022 census, about 10 per cent of the national population. Its centre is a long commercial strip called the Main Mall, with a semicircular area of government offices to its east. It holds the Bank of Botswana, the Botswana Stock Exchange and the headquarters of the Southern African Development Community, formed in 1980. The National Museum and Art Gallery, which opened in 1968, has an exhibit on the San, the earliest inhabitants of southern Africa.
gadadhar-singha: Born Gadapani Konwar, and known by the Ahom name Supatphaa, he was the son of Gobar Roja, a descendant of the king Suhungmung. The minister Debera Borbarua made Gobar king in 1675; he reigned only twenty days and was executed after Debera's fall. In 1679 Laluk Sola Borphukan had the minister Atan Burhagohain murdered, installed Sulikphaa, called Lora Roja, as king and began to hunt down the Ahom princes eligible for the throne.

To escape, Gadapani became a fugitive in the Naga hills, perhaps near the present-day Mon district, among the Konyak Naga. During this time his wife Joymoti Konwari was tortured and killed by the henchmen of Sulikphaa and Laluk Sola Borphukan. Little is known of his two years in exile, though the hills are rich in lore and legend about him.

He was formally crowned in March 1682, and bound the leading nobles to himself by marrying their daughters. His first act was to equip an army against the Mughals at Guwahati: the forts at Bansbari and Kajali fell at the first assault, and a naval victory near the mouth of the Bar Nadi delivered the whole enemy fleet to the Ahoms. The campaign ended eighty years of Ahom–Mughal conflict. He also stopped Naga raids on the border villages, partly through marriage alliances with Naga chiefs.

He built roads, among them the Dhodar Ali, 211 km long from Kamargaon to Joypur, and two stone bridges, and had a number of tanks dug. The earliest known copper plates recording grants of land by Ahom kings to Brahmins or Hindu temples date from his reign. Having met the Mughal system of land measurement while hiding in Lower Assam, he brought surveyors from Koch Bihar and Bengal; the survey began in Sivasagar and was completed only after his death.

He died in February 1696 after a reign of fourteen and a half years, leaving two sons, Lai and Lechai. Lai succeeded him under the Hindu name Rudra Singha, and under him the Ahom kingdom reached its zenith; the Tungkhungia house ruled until the end of the kingdom in 1826. Gadadhar Singha was buried at Charaideo. The American Baptist missionary Nathan Brown, who saw the royal tombs there dug open, reckoned his about ninety feet high and so natural in appearance that a stranger would have taken it for an ordinary hill.
galileo-galilei: Galileo was born in Pisa, then part of the Duchy of Florence, on 15 February 1564, the first of six children of Vincenzo Galilei, a leading lutenist, composer and music theorist, and Giulia Ammannati. His family moved to Florence when he was eight, though he stayed in Pisa for two years more. From 1575 to 1578 he was educated, particularly in logic, at the Vallombrosa Abbey. He seriously considered the priesthood, but in 1580 enrolled at the University of Pisa for a medical degree at his father's urging.

He had been deliberately kept from mathematics, since a physician earned more than a mathematician, but after accidentally attending a lecture on geometry he persuaded his reluctant father to let him study mathematics and natural philosophy instead.

Galileo made original contributions to the science of motion by combining experiments and mathematics. He was one of the first modern thinkers to state clearly that the laws of nature are mathematical. In The Assayer he wrote that philosophy is written in the book of the universe in the language of mathematics, whose characters are triangles, circles and other geometric figures. With an improved telescope he observed the Milky Way, the phases of Venus, the four largest satellites of Jupiter, Saturn's rings, lunar craters and sunspots.

His Starry Messenger of 1610 was the first scientific treatise published on observations made through a telescope. His Letters on Sunspots of 1613 suggested that the Sun and heavens are changeable. His championing of Copernican heliocentrism met opposition within the Catholic Church and from some astronomers. The Roman Inquisition investigated the matter in 1615 and concluded that his opinions contradicted accepted Biblical interpretations.

His Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems of 1632 appeared to dispute and satirise Pope Urban VIII, alienating both the Pope and the Jesuits. He was tried by the Inquisition, found vehemently suspect of heresy and forced to recant, and spent the rest of his life under house arrest. During this time he wrote Two New Sciences, published in 1638, on kinematics and the strength of materials. He died on 8 January 1642, aged 77, following a fever and heart palpitations.

Grand Duke Ferdinando II wished to bury him in the main body of the Basilica of Santa Croce, but plans were dropped after protests from Pope Urban VIII and Cardinal Francesco Barberini. He was reburied in the main body in 1737.
ganapati-kakatiya: Ganapati's father Mahadeva was killed in a conflict with the Seuna, or Yadava, kingdom in 1198–1199, and Ganapati himself was taken captive. During his captivity the kingdom suffered revolts and invasions, and the commander-in-chief Rudra of the Recherla Reddi family appears to have governed in his name. An inscription at Manthena dated 26 December 1199 calls Ganapati the establisher of all the kingdom, which suggests that he had been freed by then. Yadava inscriptions claim that their king Jaitrapala released him out of compassion; the Yadavas may rather have wanted a quiet eastern border while they fought the Hoysalas.

Helped by the decline of the Kalyani Chalukya and Chola empires, Ganapati first turned to coastal Andhra, which the Kakatiyas had lost. The Krishna delta was conquered by 1201, and his general Chaunda plundered the island of Divi, whose Ayya chiefs submitted; Ganapati married two daughters of their chief, and their brother Jayapa became his commander. The Velanati Choda ruler Prithvishvara probably died fighting the Kakatiyas about 1206, and by 1209 Vela-nadu and Kamma-nadu were annexed. At Nellore Ganapati installed the Telugu Choda chief Tikka on the throne.

Repeated campaigns in Kalinga and Vengi from 1212 against the Eastern Ganga kings Ananga Bhima III and Narasimha I had mixed results, and Kakatiya control was probably limited to the land south of the Godavari River. In 1250 an army under Samanta Bhoja won a decisive victory at Palaiyaru and restored Tikka's son Manuma-siddhi II at Nellore. Around 1257, however, the Pandya king Jatavarman Sundara I attacked; the Pandyas captured Nellore and killed Manuma-siddhi II at the Battle of Muttukuru in 1263.

Ganapati continued the removal of the capital from Anumakonda to Orugallu, where he built a fortification of 75 bastions, each protected by a nayaka, comprising a stone fort and a mud fort one within the other. He also subdued the petty chiefs who had been harassing foreign merchants at the port of Motupalli.

Ganapati apparently retired after his defeats by the Pandyas in the late 1250s. He had no male heir and two daughters, Rudrama-devi, married to the Vengi Chalukya prince Virabhadra, and Ganapama-devi. Rudrama began to rule as co-regent in 1259–1260 under the regnal name Rudra-deva Maharaja, though an inscription at Duggi shows that Ganapati was alive at least until 1269. The 17th-century Pratapa-charita says that two sons of his by junior queens, Hari-hara and Murari-deva, rebelled against her; no other source knows these sons. Inscriptions listing distant kings as his vassals follow literary convention and can be dismissed.
gautama-buddha: Siddhartha Gautama was a wandering religious teacher of the eastern Indo-Gangetic Plains who lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE. Buddhist legends place his birth at Lumbini, in what is now Nepal, to royal parents of the Shakya clan. Most scholars accept that he lived, taught and founded a monastic order during the reign of Bimbisara of Magadha and died in the reign of Bimbisara's successor Ajatashatru, making him a contemporary of Mahavira, the Jain tirthankara.

His dates are uncertain. The long chronology of the Sri Lankan chronicles gives 624 to 544 BCE, while most scholars who accept it but date Ashoka's coronation to about 268 BCE put his life at 566 to 486 BCE. The oldest surviving written mention of the Buddha is from the middle of the 3rd century BCE, in the Edicts of Ashoka, whose Lumbini pillar inscription commemorates the emperor's pilgrimage to the birthplace. The earliest biographies already contain supernatural elements, and the scholar Rupert Gethin holds that the life story is not history, nor meant to be.

According to Buddhist tradition, he renounced home life to live as a wandering ascetic and attained nirvana at Bodh Gaya in what is now Bihar. He then taught across the lower Indo-Gangetic Plain and built a monastic order, the sangha. Tradition describes a Middle Way between sensual indulgence and severe asceticism, summarised in the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path. The earliest biographical material in the Pali Nikayas describes a forty-five-year career as a teacher.

He left no writings. His teachings were compiled by the Buddhist community as the Vinaya Pitaka, on monastic discipline, and the Sutra Pitaka, discourses attributed to him, passed down orally in Middle Indo-Aryan dialects. How far later doctrine reflects his own words is disputed. Scholars such as Richard Gombrich and A. K. Warder hold that early texts contain material traceable to him, while others doubt that the beliefs of pre-sectarian Buddhism can be recovered.

Buddhist tradition holds that he died at Kushinagar, in modern Uttar Pradesh, and reached parinirvana. Buddhism later developed into the Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions and spread beyond the Indian subcontinent. It declined in India and largely disappeared there after the 8th century CE, but became more prominent in Southeast and East Asia. Mahayana sutras present Shakyamuni as a transcendent being, and the Hindu tradition incorporated the Buddha as the ninth avatar of Vishnu.

The earliest artistic depictions, at Bharhut and Sanchi, are aniconic, showing an empty throne, footprints, a Dharma wheel or a Bodhi tree. Images in human form became widespread after the first century CE, and those of Gandharan and Central Asian Buddhism were influenced by Hellenistic art, a style known as Greco-Buddhist art.
gdansk: Gdańsk lies at the mouth of the Motława River on the southern edge of Gdańsk Bay. The low-lying Lower Terrace covers part of the Vistula Fens, while the Upper Terrace is an area of uneven highlands that belongs to the Kashubian Lake District. The name most likely comes from Gdania, the old name of the Motława. Its German form, Danzig, developed from forms such as Danzc and Danczk.

The first written mention is in a biography of Saint Adalbert, which records his visit in 997 to a town called Gyddanyzc, then ruled by Bolesław I the Brave of Poland. The city grew into a trading town and later joined the Hanseatic League. In 1308 the Teutonic Knights, called in to relieve the Polish garrison, seized the town and killed many of its inhabitants; estimates of the dead range from about 60 to about 1,000. In 1454 the Prussian Confederation rejected the authority of the Teutonic Order and appealed to King Casimir IV of Poland, which led to the Thirteen Years' War, and on 16 June 1454 the king granted Danzig extensive privileges.

With considerable autonomy it served as the Polish Crown's main seaport and largest city until the early 18th century. Prussia annexed it in 1793 in the Second Partition of Poland, and it joined the German Empire in 1871. It was a free city from 1807 to 1814 and again from 1920 to 1939. A military clash at Westerplatte on 1 September 1939 was one of the first events of the Second World War. After 1945 the German population fled or was expelled and Poles settled in their place. The Solidarity trade union began in the city in the 1980s.

Gdańsk is the capital of the Pomeranian Voivodeship and Poland's sixth-largest city, with a population of 486,492, and a major seaport. With Gdynia and Sopot it forms a metropolitan area called the Tricity. Parts of the old city destroyed in the war were rebuilt in the 1950s and 1960s. Its landmarks include the Town Hall, the Green Gate, Artus Court, Neptune's Fountain and St. Mary's Church, one of the largest brick churches in the world. St. Dominic's Fair, which dates back to 1260, is still held there.
geneva: Geneva lies at the south-western end of Lake Geneva, at 46°12' North, 6°09' East, where the Rhône flows out of the lake. Three mountain chains belonging to the Jura surround it: the Jura main range to the north-west, the Vuache to the south and the Salève to the south-east. The city covers 15.93 square kilometres, and about 91.8 per cent of that land is built up.

The Canton of Geneva covers 282 square kilometres and has a border of only 4.5 kilometres with the rest of Switzerland. Of its 107.5 kilometres of border, 103 are shared with France. The name appears in Latin texts, in Caesar's spelling Genava, and probably comes from a Celtic stem meaning mouth, in the sense of an estuary.

Geneva was an Allobrogian border town, fortified against the Helvetii tribe, when the Roman Republic took it in 121 BCE. It became Christian under the Late Roman Empire. It was connected to the Bishopric of Vienne in the 4th century and acquired its own first bishop in the 5th century.

The medieval county of Geneva was known in Middle Latin as the pagus major Genevensis. After 1400 it became the Genevois province of Savoy, although the province did not extend to the city itself until the reformation of the seat of the Bishop of Geneva. A local holiday, the Jeûne genevois, falls on the first Thursday after the first Sunday in September and by tradition commemorates the day news of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of Huguenots reached the city.

Geneva is the second most populous city in Switzerland and the most populous in French-speaking Romandy. It is the capital of the Republic and Canton of Geneva. Its municipal population was 203,856 in January 2021.

The city is the European headquarters of the United Nations, in the Palace of Nations, up the hill from the headquarters of the former League of Nations. It also hosts the World Health Organization, the International Labour Organization, the International Committee of the Red Cross and CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. The whole old city is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and 82 buildings or sites are listed of national significance, among them the Cathédrale St-Pierre.
genghis-khan: Temüjin was born between 1155 and 1167, and historians favour different dates: 1155, 1162 or 1167, with 1162 accepted by most. He was the eldest child of Yesügei, a chieftain of the Borjigin clan, and Hö'elün. When he was eight his father died and his family was abandoned by its tribe. He married Börte around 1178, and when Merkit raiders kidnapped her he recovered her with armies lent by Toghrul, khan of the Kerait, and his childhood sworn brother Jamukha.

Later his relationship with Jamukha deteriorated into open warfare, and he was badly defeated around 1187. After he reappeared in 1196 he swiftly gained power, overpowered Toghrul after a surprise attack in 1203, defeated the Naiman tribe and executed Jamukha, becoming sole ruler of the Mongolian steppe.

In 1206, at a kurultai, or assembly, at the source of the Onon River, Temüjin adopted the title Genghis Khan, whose meaning is much debated. He set out to suppress tribal loyalties in favour of unconditional loyalty to the khan and the ruling family, raising his own family, the Golden Family, to the highest tier of the Mongol hierarchy.

He led a raid against the Western Xia in 1209 and fought the Jin dynasty for four years until the capture of its capital, Zhongdu, in 1215. His general Jebe annexed Qara Khitai in 1218. In 1219 Genghis invaded the Khwarazmian Empire after his envoys were executed; the campaign toppled the state and devastated Transoxiana and Khorasan, while Jebe and Subutai led an expedition that reached Georgia and Kievan Rus'. The Mongol army under him killed millions of people, yet his conquests also facilitated commercial and cultural exchange over a vast area.

Genghis fell from his horse while hunting in the winter of 1226 to 1227 and grew ill during the siege of Zhongxing, the Western Xia capital. He died on 18 or 25 August 1227, and Zhongxing fell the following month, its population treated with extreme savagery. He was buried on or near Burkhan Khaldun in the Khentii Mountains, a site he had chosen years before.

His son Ögedei acceded in 1229. The division of the empire into appanages, meant to ensure stability, had the opposite effect, and in the late 1200s it split into the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty. He is remembered as a savage tyrant in Russia and the Arab world, while modern Mongolians recognise him as the founding father of their nation.
geoffrey-chaucer: Geoffrey Chaucer was born in London, most likely in the early 1340s; his monument gives 1343, but the precise date and place are unknown. His father, John Chaucer, rose to be an important wine merchant with a royal appointment, and earlier generations of the family had been vintners and merchants in Ipswich. The surname derives from the French chaucier, a maker of shoes, boots or leggings. In 1357 the first of the Chaucer Life Records shows him as a page in the household of Elizabeth de Burgh, Countess of Ulster, whose husband Lionel of Antwerp was a son of Edward III; the post brought him into the court circle in which he stayed for the rest of his life.

Chaucer was a public servant whose official life is very well documented, with nearly 500 written items. He worked as a courtier, a diplomat and a civil servant, sat in the Parliament of England as shire knight for Kent, and was Clerk of the King's Works from 1389 to 1391. He was a close friend of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, and served under his patronage; in 1366 he married Philippa de Roet, and when Lancaster married her sister Katherine Swynford in 1396 the two men became brothers-in-law.

His first major work was The Book of the Duchess, an elegy for Blanche of Lancaster, who died in 1368. He wrote many of his major works while he was customs comptroller for London, from 1374 to 1386, among them the Parlement of Foules, The Legend of Good Women and Troilus and Criseyde, and he is believed to have begun The Canterbury Tales in the 1380s. He also translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy and wrote A Treatise on the Astrolabe for his ten-year-old son Lewis.

Chaucer died on 25 October 1400 and was the first writer buried in what has since become Poets' Corner in Westminster Abbey. He invented the rhyme royal and was one of the first English poets to use the five-stress line. His contemporary Thomas Hoccleve called him the first finder of our fair language, and almost two thousand English words are first attested in his manuscripts. Eighty-three manuscripts of The Canterbury Tales survive, in whole or part, and William Caxton, the first English printer, published two folio editions of it, in 1478 and 1483.
georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel: Hegel was born on 27 August 1770 in Stuttgart, capital of the Duchy of Württemberg. His father, Georg Ludwig Hegel, was secretary to the revenue office at the court of Karl Eugen, Duke of Württemberg. His mother died of bilious fever when he was thirteen; he and his father also caught the disease but narrowly survived. At Stuttgart's Eberhard-Ludwigs-Gymnasium, which he entered in 1776, he read voraciously. His first biographer, Karl Rosenkranz, wrote that the school belonged entirely to the Enlightenment in principle and entirely to classical antiquity in curriculum. Entering the Tübingen seminary in 1788, he was more devoted to the classics than to anything modern, and the Greeks, especially Plato, came first.

In 1801 Hegel came to Jena at the encouragement of Schelling and became a Privatdozent after submitting the dissertation De Orbitis Planetarum. In 1802 he and Schelling founded the Critical Journal of Philosophy, a collaboration that ended when Schelling left for Würzburg in 1803. In 1805 he was promoted to an unsalaried extraordinary professorship. With his finances failing, he was finishing the Phenomenology of Spirit as Napoleon engaged Prussian troops in the Battle of Jena on 14 October 1806. The book appeared in 1807 and was poorly understood even by his contemporaries.

His academic career culminated in the chair of philosophy at the University of Berlin, where he remained a prominent figure until his death on 14 November 1831. From 1818 he lectured there on the philosophy of art as an autonomous subject.

His system has three parts: the science of logic, the philosophy of nature and the philosophy of spirit, a structure drawn from Proclus's triad of remaining, procession and return and from the Christian Trinity. Geist, usually rendered spirit, denotes the human mind and its products, and Hegel held that the essence of spirit is freedom. His method, often called dialectical, he usually called speculative. The scheme of thesis, antithesis and synthesis comes from Fichte; Walter Kaufmann notes that Hegel never used the three terms together.

History was central to his philosophy: a culture is more advanced the more it is permeated by awareness of freedom. After his death his followers split into Right and Left Hegelians. The Left, including Ludwig Feuerbach and Karl Marx, adapted his method for materialist critiques of religion and society.
george-frideric-handel: Handel was born in 1685 in Halle, in the Duchy of Magdeburg, then part of Brandenburg-Prussia, in the same year as Johann Sebastian Bach and Domenico Scarlatti. His father, Georg Händel, was an eminent barber-surgeon who served the court of Saxe-Weissenfels. Almost everything known of his childhood comes from his first biographer, John Mainwaring, who often relates misinformation, including the portrait of the father as implacably opposed to a musical education.

Between the ages of seven and nine Handel went with his father to Weissenfels, where Duke Johann Adolf I heard him play the court organ and recommended that he be taught. His only teacher was Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the Halle parish church. His father died on 11 February 1697, and in 1702 Handel matriculated at the University of Halle. By July 1703 he was in Hamburg, and he then went to Italy.

In June 1710 Handel became Kapellmeister to George, the Elector of Hanover, but left at the end of the year for London, where his opera Rinaldo was a great success. He settled there in 1712. In 1717 he became house composer at Cannons in Middlesex, where he wrote the Chandos Anthems and Acis and Galatea. From 1719 he engaged singers for the Royal Academy of Music, founded by aristocrats to secure a steady supply of Italian opera. By 1723 he lived at 25 Brook Street, now the Handel House Museum.

He started three commercial opera companies, the third at Covent Garden in 1734. In 1737 he suffered a physical breakdown and turned towards English choral works, and after the success of Messiah in 1742 he never composed an Italian opera again. In 1749 he wrote Music for the Royal Fireworks, whose first performance drew 12,000 people, and in 1750 he arranged a performance of Messiah for the Foundling Hospital. He died on 14 April 1759, aged 74, and was given a state funeral at Westminster Abbey.

Handel's compositions include 42 operas, 24 oratorios, more than 120 cantatas, 18 concerti grossi and 12 organ concertos. His first oratorio, an allegory, was composed in Italy in 1707. One of his four coronation anthems, Zadok the Priest, has been performed at every British coronation since 1727. His music was admired by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven.
george-i-of-greece: He was born Prince William of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Glücksburg on 24 December 1845 at the Yellow Palace in Copenhagen, the second son of Prince Christian and Princess Louise of Hesse-Kassel. The family was relatively obscure until 1852, when his father was designated heir to the childless Frederick VII of Denmark. William entered the Royal Danish Navy as a cadet.

After the expulsion of Otto in October 1862 the Greeks held a plebiscite in which Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, a son of Queen Victoria, received over 95 per cent of the 240,000 votes; William received six. The ruling families of the great powers were barred from the Greek crown, and the choice fell on the Danish prince. The Greek National Assembly elected him unanimously on 30 March 1863.

George reached Athens on 30 October 1863, learned Greek quickly and was often seen informally in the streets. He sent home Danish advisers who had become unpopular, and in October 1864 pressed the Assembly to finish its work; on 28 November he swore to a constitution that created a single chamber, the Vouli, elected by direct, secret, universal male suffrage. Governments were short-lived: 21 between 1864 and 1874. After Charilaos Trikoupis blamed the king in a newspaper article for imposing minority governments, George declared in 1875 that the leader of the parliamentary majority would in future be appointed prime minister.

Trikoupis and Theodoros Deligiannis alternated in office between 1882 and 1897. In 1896 the king presided over the opening of the revived Olympic Games in Athens. A revolt in Crete led in 1897 to a war with the Ottoman Empire that was lost by the end of April; Greece paid an indemnity of 4 million Turkish pounds and Crete passed to international administration. George considered abdication, but regained esteem after he and his daughter Maria survived an attack by two riflemen on 27 February 1898.

In August 1909 a league of army officers demanded that the royal family lose their military commissions and attempted a coup. George gave way to calls for a revising assembly, and Eleftherios Venizelos became prime minister in 1910. King and minister agreed on rebuilding the army, which entered Thessaloniki on 9 November 1912 under Crown Prince Constantine. On 18 March 1913, walking near the White Tower without meaningful protection, George was shot in the back by Alexandros Schinas and died at once. Schinas fell to his death from a police station window six weeks later. The dynasty he founded reigned, with breaks, until the monarchy was abolished in 1973.
george-orwell: Eric Arthur Blair was born on 25 June 1903 in Motihari, Bengal Presidency, British India, into what he described as a lower-upper-middle-class family. His father, Richard Walmesley Blair, worked in the Opium Department of the Indian Civil Service, and his mother, Ida Mabel Blair, grew up in Moulmein, Burma. When he was one year old his mother took him and his sister Marjorie to England, and in 1904 she settled at Henley-on-Thames. Apart from a brief visit in mid-1907, he did not see his father until 1912.

He attended a convent school in Henley run by French Ursuline nuns, and then, through a scholarship, St Cyprian's School in Eastbourne from September 1911. He hated the school and later wrote the essay Such, Such Were the Joys about it, published after his death. He met Cyril Connolly there. He went on to win a scholarship to Eton. As a child he took a keen interest in natural history, in butterflies, birds and fishing, and his adult diaries are full of observations of nature.

Blair wrote under the pen name George Orwell. For most of his career he was best known for journalism, in essays, reviews, columns and books of reportage: Down and Out in Paris and London, The Road to Wigan Pier (1937), on the living conditions of the poor in northern England, and Homage to Catalonia (1938), on his experiences soldiering for the Republican side in the Spanish Civil War. He later called that war his watershed political experience, and said that everything he had written since 1936 was directed against totalitarianism and for democratic socialism.

Modern readers meet him more often as a novelist, through the allegorical novella Animal Farm (1945), often thought to reflect the degeneration of the Soviet Union and the rise of Stalinism, and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), on life under totalitarian rule. Many of his coinages, such as Big Brother, Thought Police, Room 101, Newspeak and doublethink, entered the English language. He was an atheist who identified with the humanist outlook, yet he took part in the life of the Church of England. His works are widely studied in schools in England, and his political legacy is contested, with critics on both left and right claiming or attacking him.
george-washington: George Washington was born on 22 February 1732 (11 February 1731 in the old style calendar) at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia, the first of six children of Augustine and Mary Ball Washington. When his father died in 1743 he inherited Ferry Farm and ten slaves, while his half-brother Lawrence inherited the estate renamed Mount Vernon. Without the formal schooling his half-brothers had in England, he learned mathematics and land surveying and became a talented draftsman and mapmaker.

Lawrence's service as adjutant general of the Virginia militia inspired him to seek a commission. His report was published in Virginia and London. On 6 January 1759 he married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow, and became one of the wealthiest men in Virginia.

After the war began with Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775, the Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army on 14 June, and John Adams nominated Washington as its commander-in-chief. He led a poorly organised force against disciplined British troops. He won at Boston in March 1776 but was forced to retreat from New York City in November. He crossed the Delaware River and won at Trenton in late 1776 and Princeton in early 1777, then lost at Brandywine and Germantown. In 1781 he led a combined French and American force to a decisive victory at Yorktown, and the Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognised American independence.

He presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787. Elected unanimously by the Electoral College in 1789 and 1792, he was inaugurated on 30 April 1789 at Federal Hall in New York City. President against grander styles proposed by the Senate. He stayed neutral in the rivalry between Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton in his cabinet, and adopted neutrality during the French Revolution while supporting the Jay Treaty with Britain.

Washington's farewell address of 1796 stressed national unity and the dangers of regionalism, partisanship and foreign influence. In 1798 President Adams made him commanding general of the army during the Quasi-War, though he did not take the field. He died on 14 December 1799, and Henry Lee III eulogised him as first in war, first in peace and first in the hearts of his countrymen.

At least 577 slaves lived and worked at Mount Vernon during his lifetime. From the 1760s he gradually grew to oppose slavery, partly because his shift from tobacco to grain left him with a costly surplus of slaves, and in a letter of 1778 he wrote of his desire to get quit of Negroes. His will provided for the eventual manumission of his slaves.
georgetown-guyana: Georgetown is on the east bank of the Demerara River estuary, on Guyana's Atlantic coast, in flat coastal plains. The city is surrounded by cane fields and marshy swamps, with savannah to the east and south. Its land lies as much as 2 metres below the high-tide level, and a retaining wall known as the seawall keeps the ocean out, while a network of canals with kokers, or sluices, built by the Dutch and later the British, drains the city. It is laid out in a north-south, east-west grid interlaced with these canals. It has a hot, trade-wind tropical rainforest climate, moderated by the north-east trade winds, and rarely sees temperatures above 31 degrees Celsius.

In 1748 Governor Laurens Storm van 's Gravesande built a guard post at the mouth of the Demerara River, and English planters later built houses around it, forming a small village. The town was established in 1782 during a brief French occupation of the Dutch colony of Demerara, under the name Longchamps. In 1784 the name was changed to Stabroek, after Nicholaas Geelvinck, Lord of Stabroek, then President of the Dutch West India Company. In 1789 the population was 780, of whom 239 were white, but the town grew quickly, reaching around 8,500 by 1807. American traders built a wharf that became known as American Stelling.

Under British rule the city took the name Georgetown in 1812, in honour of King George III. A ward one fourth of a mile broad and one mile long retains the name Stabroek. Georgetown gained official city status on 24 August 1842, in the reign of Queen Victoria. A large fire, the Great Fire, caused widespread damage in 1945.

Georgetown is the capital and largest city of Guyana, the seat of its government and the home of the Secretariat of the Caribbean Community, CARICOM. The 2022 census recorded 125,683 people. It is known for its colonial architecture, with many wooden buildings and markets. These include the tall painted-timber St. George's Anglican Cathedral, State House (built 1852), the neo-Gothic City Hall (1889), the Victoria Law Courts (1887), the Parliament Building (1829-1834) and Stabroek Market (1792), whose cast-iron clock tower dominates the skyline. The Georgetown Cenotaph, built in 1923, is the site of Remembrance Day services each November.
germania: Roman geographers placed Germania roughly between the Rhine in the west and the Vistula in the east, from the upper Danube northwards along the North and Baltic seas to the known parts of southern Scandinavia. The free lands are also called Magna Germania, and by modern scholars Germania Libera or the Germanic Barbaricum. The origin of the name Germani is uncertain. Tacitus wrote that the name had once belonged only to the Tungri, west of the Rhine, and was later extended to supposedly related peoples beyond it.

The country held many peoples with little unity among them, and river names suggest that another Indo-European group lived there, probably under Germanic domination. Archaeologically it corresponds, from the 1st to the 4th century CE, to the Roman Iron Age: largely agrarian, without cities or coinage of its own. Amber was a primary export, and Roman luxury goods were imported on a large scale and have been found as far away as Scandinavia and western Russia.

Julius Caesar met peoples from beyond the Rhine during the Gallic Wars and called their homeland Germania, a name the Romans appear to have borrowed from the Gauls. Augustus later carried Roman arms as far as the Elbe and in 7 BCE created a short-lived province, Germania Antiqua, before the victory of Arminius ended the attempt. The Rhine became the frontier. Germani such as the Ubii and Sicambri were settled on the Roman bank, which was heavily affected by the Revolt of the Batavi under Gaius Julius Civilis in 69–70 CE.

Under the Flavian dynasty the two provinces were organised, Germania Inferior with its headquarters at Colonia, the modern Cologne, and Germania Superior at Mogontiacum. The Romans also occupied the land between the Rhine, Main and Danube, known as the Agri Decumates. In the 3rd century confederations such as the Alemanni and Franks emerged and raided the provinces, and around 280 CE the Agri Decumates were evacuated and taken by the Alemanni. In 406 a large number of people fleeing the Huns crossed the Rhine, and Roman rule there eventually collapsed.

Much of Germania, including all the former Roman provinces, was eventually incorporated into the Frankish Empire and later East Francia. The name survived in learned use: it is attested in Old English translations of Bede and Orosius, and since the 17th century the usual English name of Germany has been derived from it, as are the names of that country in many other languages.
germany: Ancient humans were present in what is now Germany at least 600,000 years ago. Germanic peoples expanded from southern Scandinavia and northern Germany, and the Celtic-speaking peoples of the south were later assimilated by them. Under Augustus, the Roman Empire created a short-lived province of Germania between the Rhine and Elbe rivers, and in 9 CE Arminius defeated three Roman legions in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, an outcome that dissuaded the Romans from conquering Germania. After the invasion of the Huns in 375 and the decline of Rome from 395, the Franks established the Frankish Kingdom.

Charlemagne founded the Carolingian Empire in 800, and after its division in 843 the Kingdom of Germany and the Holy Roman Empire emerged from the eastern successor kingdom of East Francia. Northern German regions became the centre of the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century. After the Holy Roman Empire's dissolution in 1806 the German Confederation was formed in 1815, and Prussia led unification into the German Empire in 1871. The Weimar Republic replaced the Empire after World War I. The Nazi rise to power in 1933 led to a totalitarian dictatorship under Adolf Hitler, which resulted in World War II and the Holocaust.

In 1949, after the war and Allied occupation, Germany was organised into two polities with limited sovereignty: the Federal Republic of Germany, or West Germany, and the German Democratic Republic, or East Germany. The first was a founding member of the European Economic Community, while the second was a communist Eastern Bloc state and a founding member of the Warsaw Pact. The former East German states joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990, and Germany regained its full sovereignty on 15 March 1991.

Germany covers 357,022 square kilometres between the Baltic Sea and the North Sea in the north and the Alps in the south, and its highest point is the Zugspitze at 2,963 metres. It is a federal parliamentary republic of sixteen Länder under the Basic Law of 1949, and Berlin is the capital and most populous city. The census of 2023 recorded a population of 84.7 million. Four national minorities live in the country: a Danish minority, the Sorbs, the Roma and Sinti, and the Frisians.
ghana: Ghana lies on the Gulf of Guinea, a few degrees north of the Equator, and covers 239,567 square kilometres with an Atlantic coastline of about 560 kilometres. It borders Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso and Togo. The land consists of low coastal plains, forested hills in the centre, and savanna in the north. The Prime Meridian passes through Tema, near Accra. Lake Volta, formed by the Akosombo Dam completed in 1965, is the largest reservoir in the world by surface area. The highest point is Mount Afadja, at 885 metres, in the Akwapim-Togo Range.

The earliest kingdoms to emerge were Bonoman in the south, existing in the 11th century, and the Kingdom of Dagbon in the north. From the 17th century Akan states, mainly based on gold trading, emerged from what is believed to have been the Bonoman area; they included Adansi, Asante, Denkyira, Akyem and Akwamu. By the 19th century the south was included in the Asante Kingdom, whose government grew from a loose network into a centralised kingdom with a specialised bureaucracy centred on Kumasi.

The Portuguese came to the Gold Coast in the 15th century to trade, and in 1481 King John II of Portugal commissioned Diogo de Azambuja to build Elmina Castle. The Dutch joined the gold trade by 1598 and captured Elmina in 1617. The British eventually controlled the coast by the 19th century. The modern borders took shape after more than a century of colonial resistance and joined four British territories: the Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland.

On 6 March 1957 Ghana became the first colony in Sub-Saharan Africa to achieve sovereignty. Under President Kwame Nkrumah it became influential in decolonisation and the Pan-African movement. Ghana alternated between civilian and military governments until January 1993, when the Fourth Republic began after elections in late 1992.

The name comes from Wagadu, an empire of west Africa from the 3rd to 12th centuries that Arab traders called Ghana; it is thought to derive from the title Kaya Maghan, meaning ruler of gold. According to Jack Goody, the idea that the Akan descended from the medieval empire lacked linguistic and historical evidence, yet became influential among nationalist intellectuals. The name was adopted as a symbol of precolonial prestige before independence. English is the official language.
ghent: Ghent lies at the confluence of the Scheldt and the Leie, in the East Flanders province of the Flemish Region of Belgium. Archaeological evidence shows human presence there from the Stone Age and Iron Age. Most historians derive the older name, Ganda, from a Celtic word meaning confluence or river mouth, while other sources connect it with an obscure deity named Gontia. The rivers flowed through land that flooded periodically, and these water-meadows were well suited to grazing sheep, whose wool fed the city's cloth trade.

Around 650 Saint Amand founded two abbeys in Ghent, St. Peter's and St. Bavo's, and around 800 Louis the Pious appointed Einhard, the biographer of Charlemagne, abbot of both. The city grew from the abbeys and a commercial centre, and Vikings plundered it in 851 and 879. Under the protection of the County of Flanders it flourished from the 11th century as a small city-state. By the 13th century it was the biggest city in Europe north of the Alps after Paris, with up to 65,000 people within its walls, and the leading centre of woollen cloth manufacture; by the middle of that century the industry employed 4,000 weavers and 1,200 fullers.

In 1453 Ghent suffered a heavy defeat at the Battle of Gavere at the hands of Philip the Good, after high taxes had led to rebellion. Afterwards the political and social centre of the Low Countries began to shift from Flanders towards Brabant. After the Revolt of Ghent in 1539, Charles V, a native of the city, made its nobles walk before him barefoot with a noose around the neck, so that its people have since been called Stroppendragers, or noose bearers. St. Bavo's Abbey was torn down and replaced with a fortress for Spanish troops. The Eighty Years' War ended Ghent's role as a centre of international importance.

Ghent's textile industry flourished again in the 18th and 19th centuries, and in 1800 Lieven Bauwens introduced the first mechanical weaving machine on the European continent after smuggling plans out of England. The Treaty of Ghent, adopted on Christmas Eve 1814, formally ended the War of 1812 between Great Britain and the United States. The city was occupied by the Germans in both world wars but escaped severe destruction, and was liberated on 6 September 1944.

Ghent is the capital and largest city of its province and the third largest city in Belgium, a port and university city. Much of its medieval architecture survives, including St. Bavo's Cathedral with the Ghent Altarpiece, the belfry, the Gravensteen castle and the buildings along the old Graslei harbour. UNESCO recognised its béguinages as World Heritage Sites in 1998, and the belfry and adjacent cloth hall in 1999.
giacomo-puccini: Giacomo Puccini was born in Lucca, then in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the sixth of nine children of Michele Puccini and Albina Magi. His great-great-grandfather, also named Giacomo, had made the family a local musical dynasty as maestro di cappella of the Cattedrale di San Martino, a post passed down through his son Antonio, his grandson Domenico and Michele. Each studied music at Bologna and composed church music, and Domenico and Michele also wrote operas. Michele's funeral was an occasion of public mourning.

At the Milan Conservatory, Puccini studied under Ponchielli and Bazzini. His thesis piece, the Capriccio sinfonico, was performed on 14 July 1883 and favourably reviewed. His first opera, Le Villi, was entered for a competition run by the publisher Sonzogno but was disqualified because its manuscript was illegible. The publisher Giulio Ricordi then commissioned Edgar, which premiered at La Scala on 21 April 1889 to a lukewarm response and never became popular. Ricordi kept Puccini on and continued his allowance. Manon Lescaut was completed with the librettists Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa.

La bohème, based on Henri Murger's La Vie de Bohème, premiered in Turin in 1896 under Arturo Toscanini and was soon performed in leading opera houses in Europe and the United States. Tosca followed in 1900, arguably his first venture into verismo, the realistic depiction of life including violence. Madama Butterfly, first given at La Scala on 17 February 1904, was greeted with hostility, probably owing to inadequate rehearsals; Puccini withdrew it and revised it, and a fifth version of 1907 became the standard one.

La fanciulla del West, from a play by David Belasco, premiered at the Metropolitan Opera in New York on 10 December 1910, the first world premiere of an opera there. La rondine was first given at Monte Carlo on 27 March 1917, and Il trittico, three one-act operas, in New York in 1918. Puccini left Turandot unfinished; Franco Alfano completed the last two scenes from his sketches.

In 1903 Puccini was seriously injured in a car crash on the road from Lucca to Torre del Lago, where he had a villa on the lake from about 1900, and he was found to have a form of diabetes. Late in 1923 he began to complain of a sore throat, and doctors diagnosed throat cancer and recommended an experimental radiation treatment in Brussels. He died there on 29 November 1924, aged 65, of complications after the treatment. News reached Rome during a performance of La bohème, which was stopped while the orchestra played Chopin's Funeral March. He is buried in a chapel at the Villa Puccini.
gibraltar: Gibraltar lies near the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, on the Bay of Gibraltar, close to where the Mediterranean Sea meets the Atlantic Ocean at the Strait of Gibraltar. Its territory covers 6.8 square kilometres and shares a land border of 1.2 kilometres with Spain. The Rock of Gibraltar dominates the landscape, and the town stands at its foot. The name comes from the Arabic Jabal Ṭāriq, the Mount of Tariq, after the eighth-century North African commander Tariq ibn Ziyad, who began the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula across the strait in 711.

Neanderthals lived in Gorham's Cave about 50,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens went on using the caves of Gibraltar from about 40,000 years ago to about 5,000 years ago. Neolithic pottery found in the caves is mostly of the Almerian culture of Andalusia. There is little evidence of habitation in the Bronze Age, when people had largely stopped living in caves.

The Almohads founded Gibraltar as a permanent watchtower in 1160. In the Late Middle Ages control passed between the Nasrids, Castilians and Marinids, and the place gained strategic weight with the destruction of nearby Algeciras around 1375. It became part of the Crown of Castile again in 1462. Anglo-Dutch forces captured it from Spain in 1704, during the War of the Spanish Succession, and it was ceded to Great Britain in perpetuity by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

Its control of the narrow entrance to the Mediterranean made it an important base for the Royal Navy, particularly during the Napoleonic Wars and the Second World War. Gibraltar was declared a crown colony on 25 June 1830. Water was a constant concern: with no rivers or streams, the town relied on wells, cisterns and rainwater, and in the late nineteenth century a Sanitary Commission introduced large-scale desalination and giant catchments after cholera and yellow fever had spread. In 1969 Francisco Franco closed the land frontier with Spain, and it reopened in 1982.

Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with almost complete internal self-government through an elected parliament, while the United Kingdom remains responsible for defence and foreign policy. Spain asserts a claim to the territory; Gibraltarians overwhelmingly rejected Spanish sovereignty in a referendum in 1967 and shared sovereignty in 2002. English is the language of government, commerce and education, and many Gibraltarians also speak Spanish and a local dialect called Llanito. About 38,000 people live there, and their ancestry includes Genoese, Maltese, Portuguese, Sephardic Jewish and Moroccan as well as Spanish and British.
giovanni-boccaccio: Boccaccio was the son of the Florentine merchant Boccaccino di Chellino and an unknown woman, and was probably born out of wedlock. He grew up in Florence, where his father worked for the Compagnia dei Bardi, and may have been tutored by Giovanni Mazzuoli, who gave him an early introduction to the works of Dante. In 1326 his father was appointed head of a bank and the family moved to Naples. Boccaccio disliked banking and studied canon law at the Studium for six years, while pursuing scientific and literary studies and meeting scholars and the Neapolitan nobility.

In Naples Boccaccio began what he considered his true vocation, poetry. Il Filostrato and the Teseida of this period were the sources for Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde and The Knight's Tale. He returned to Florence in early 1341, after tensions between the Angevin king and Florence, and his father, who had gone bankrupt, died in 1349. He began the Decameron around 1349; the choice of a hundred tales and the frame story of three men and seven women dates from this time. It was largely complete by 1352 and revised in 1370-1371.

From 1350 he was closely involved with humanism and with the Florentine government, which sent him on missions to Romagna, Brandenburg, Milan and Avignon. He housed Leontius Pilatus and encouraged his tentative translations of Homer, Euripides and Aristotle. In October 1350 he welcomed Francesco Petrarch to Florence, and Petrarch became his teacher and friend. Their discussions fed the Genealogia deorum gentilium, completed in 1360, a reference work on classical mythology that defended the study of ancient literature against clerical intellectuals who wished to limit it. In 1360 he began De mulieribus claris, biographies of 106 women, completed in 1374, and in 1373 he lectured on Dante, which produced his Esposizioni sopra la Commedia di Dante.

Illness troubled Boccaccio's last years. He died on 21 December 1375 in Certaldo, where he is buried, and his library passed to the monastery of Santo Spirito in Florence. He is counted with Dante and Petrarch as one of the Three Crowns of Italian literature. Pietro Bembo made his style a model of Italian prose in the sixteenth century, and he influenced Chaucer, Miguel de Cervantes and Lope de Vega.
giovanni-giustiniani-longo: Giustiniani, born in 1418, belonged to the House of Giustiniani and was probably a native of Chios. That he lived as a mercenary suggests he was not the first-born son of his family. He left no testimony of his reasons for going to Constantinople. Reportedly Emperor Constantine XI promised him sovereignty over the island of Lemnos in case of victory.

Constantine XI gave him the rank of protostrator. Why he in particular was chosen is unclear; one explanation offered is that the emperor distrusted the city's large and discontented Venetian population and preferred a Genoese. Giustiniani trained the recruits, strengthened the fortifications and brought back men who had fled to monasteries to escape military duty. Drawing on the siege of 1422, he concentrated the defence on the outer walls. Some 8,000 to 9,000 people were available to defend the city, and his own post was at the lowest-lying section of the walls, between the gates of St. Romanos and Charisius.

After Sultan Mehmed II arrived on 6 April, Giustiniani led sorties that destroyed Ottoman troops, siege works and artillery, until their cost in lives caused them to be given up. Against the Ottoman guns, which included a cannon 6 metres long, he had the walls covered with soft surfaces and the breaches filled with debris, into which the cannonballs sank. On 18 April his men repelled the first assault, by Janissaries and archers at a narrow breach, after four hours.

In the final assault of 29 May two waves were beaten back before the Janissaries attacked a line held by no more than 3,000 exhausted troops. The accounts differ on his wound: a cannon shot or a crossbow bolt struck his arm, chest or leg. He was taken to his ship and sailed away with his men when the fall of the city became known. He died on 1 June and was buried in the church of San Domenico in the Castle of Chios. The tomb is lost, possibly destroyed in the earthquake of 1881, though descriptions of its inscription survive.

Sources hostile to the Genoese, above all the Venetian eyewitness Nicolò Barbaro, claim that he was lightly wounded or not at all and left his post out of fear. The charges of cowardice and treason spread so widely that the Republic of Genoa denied them in letters to the chanceries of England, France, the Duchy of Burgundy and others. The historians Marios Philippides and Walter Hanak rebut Barbaro, citing several other sources that record an injury.
giuseppe-verdi: Verdi was the first child of Carlo Giuseppe Verdi and Luigia Uttini, an innkeeper and a spinner according to the baptismal register of 11 October 1813. He was born at Le Roncole, near Busseto, then in the Taro department of the First French Empire, and from the age of four had private lessons in Latin and Italian. He learned the organ and showed so much interest in music that his parents gave him a spinet. With the help of a local patron, Antonio Barezzi, he received a musical education. In 1835 he became director of the Busseto school, and the La Scala impresario Bartolomeo Merelli agreed to stage his first opera, Oberto, in November 1839.

Nabucco, in 1842, made his reputation, and I Lombardi alla prima crociata followed in 1843. Verdi then wrote twenty operas over sixteen years, a period he later called sixteen years in the galleys. Rigoletto, based on Victor Hugo's Le roi s'amuse, was written for Venice in 1851, and with Il trovatore and La traviata it cemented his fame. Censors objected to Stiffelio and Rigoletto, and Verdi refused to compromise on the hunchbacked hero of the latter.

After La traviata he wrote only six new stage works in eighteen years, up to Aida, and he returned happily to his estate at Sant'Agata. In 1859 he began to take an active interest in Italian politics, and he served briefly as an elected politician. After the success of Otello in 1887 he said that having massacred so many heroes and heroines he had the right to laugh a little, and with a libretto by Boito he wrote the comedy Falstaff, of 1893.

Critics divide Verdi's work into early, middle and late periods. Macbeth of 1847 has been called his first masterpiece, and his late masterpieces are the Requiem of 1874 and the operas Otello and Falstaff. He was influenced by Rossini, Bellini and Donizetti and by the French Grand opera of Meyerbeer and Spontini.

Historians debate how political his operas were. The chorus Va, pensiero from Nabucco became an anthem of Italian patriots, and from 1859 the slogan Viva VERDI was used as an acronym for Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia. The music historian Philip Gossett notes that myths exaggerating his early nationalism circulated in the nineteenth century: the audience is said to have demanded an encore of Va, pensiero at its Milan premiere, but the piece encored was in fact the hymn Immenso Jehova.
glasgow: Glasgow lies on the banks of the River Clyde in west central Scotland, with the Kelvin as an important tributary. The name is Brittonic in origin, from glas, meaning grey-green or grey-blue, and a second element meaning hollow, giving a sense of green hollow; it is often said to mean dear green place, and the dear green place remains an affectionate name for the city. The area around Glasgow has hosted communities for millennia and the Romans built outposts there and the Antonine Wall.

Glasgow grew from a small rural settlement near its cathedral into a medieval bishopric and burgh, and was raised to the status of Royal Burgh in 1611. Its early trade was in agriculture, brewing and fishing, and from 1668 the magistrates created a deep water port at Port Glasgow, down the Clyde, because the river was then too shallow for seagoing merchant ships.

After the Acts of Union in 1707 Glasgow became prominent as a hub of trade with the Americas, in sugar, tobacco, cotton and manufactured goods. The city prospered from the triangular trade and the Atlantic slave trade on which it depended, and its merchants dealt in slave-produced crops. From 1717 to 1766 Scottish slave ships, mainly sailing from Greenock and Port Glasgow, carried approximately 3,000 enslaved Africans to the Americas. By the late 18th century more than half of the British tobacco trade was concentrated on the Clyde. The city became a major centre of the Scottish Enlightenment.

As the population grew, about 4,000 people died in an outbreak of cholera in 1848–1849, which led to the Loch Katrine aqueduct, 26 miles long, opened by Queen Victoria in 1859. The population reached 1,034,174 in 1921 and peaked at 1,127,825 in 1938, and boundary extensions between 1912 and 1936 tripled the city's area. In the First World War approximately 18,000 Glaswegian soldiers were lost. Clearance of poor inner-city areas such as the Gorbals and resettlement in new towns including Cumbernauld and East Kilbride reduced the population from the 1960s.

Glasgow is the most populous city in Scotland and one of its 32 unitary council areas, administered by Glasgow City Council. Its cultural institutions include the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery, the Burrell Collection, Scottish Opera and Scottish Ballet, and it was European Capital of Culture in 1990. St. Mungo's Cathedral, of the 13th century, and Provand's Lordship, of the 15th, are the two main landmarks of the medieval city.
goa: Goa lies on the southwestern coast of India, in the Konkan region, separated from the Deccan highlands by the Western Ghats. It covers 3,702 square kilometres, and its highest point, Sonsogor, rises to 1,167 metres. The climate is tropical monsoon, with over 90 per cent of the rain falling from June to September. Rock engravings at Usgalimal and Kajur are among the earliest known traces of human life in India.

In the 3rd century BCE Goa belonged to the Maurya Empire under Ashoka. Between the 2nd century BCE and the 6th century CE it was ruled by the Bhojas of Goa, then by the Chalukyas of Badami from 578 to 753 and the Rashtrakutas from 753 to 963. The Kadambas, who followed as feudatories of the Chalukyas of Kalyani, patronised Jainism.

In 1510 the Portuguese defeated the Bijapur sultan Yusuf Adil Shah with the help of a local ally, Thimmayya or Timoji, and set up a permanent settlement at Old Goa. Under Afonso de Albuquerque the city became capital of the Estado da Índia. The Goa Inquisition was established in 1560 and abolished in 1812, and the first printing press in India produced its first books in 1556. Old Goa was abandoned in the 19th century after outbreaks of disease. On 19 December 1961 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Vijay and annexed Goa, and on 30 May 1987 it became India's twenty-fifth state.

Goa is a state of India with Panaji as its capital and Vasco da Gama as its largest city. Konkani is its sole official language, with Marathi also permitted for official purposes. The census of 2011 counted 1,458,545 people, 66.1 per cent of them Hindu and 25.1 per cent Christian. The Bom Jesus Basilica and the churches and convents of Old Goa form its World Heritage Site; the basilica holds the remains of Saint Francis Xavier. Goan cooking, based on rice, fish and coconut, is heavily influenced by Portuguese cuisine.
gorgan: The present city of Gorgan is the capital of Golestan province and lies about 400 km north-east of Tehran and some 30 km from the Caspian Sea. North of it stretches the wide Dasht-e Gorgan, the Plain of Gorgan. The city has hot, humid summers and cool, wet winters, with about 584 millimetres of rain a year, while the Gorgan valley has a semi-arid climate. Some 150 km to the east is the Golestan National Park.

More than 50 archaeological sites lie on the Gorgan Plain, among them Tureng Tepe and Shah Tepe, with remains from the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods. According to the Greek historian Arrian, Zadracarta was the largest city of Hyrcania and the site of its royal palace. Hyrcania became part of the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great or his successor Cambyses. The Great Wall of Gorgan was built in the Parthian and Sasanian periods, and under the Sasanians the name Gurgan was used for a city, a provincial capital and a province.

The region kept its independence as a Zoroastrian state even after the Arab conquest of Persia in the 7th century. In 1210 the city was invaded and sacked by the army of the Kingdom of Georgia under the Mkhargrdzeli brothers. Old Gorgan was destroyed during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, and the centre of the region moved to Astarabad, which is the city now called Gorgan. Astarabad was an important political and religious city in the Qajar era.

The census of 2016 counted 350,676 people in the city, against 269,226 in 2006. It has several universities, among them Golestan University and Gorgan University. Among the people the city counts as its own are the 11th-century poet Fakhroddin Asaad Gorgani, composer of Vis and Ramin, the 11th-century grammarian Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, and Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, Shah of Iran from 1789 to 1797.
gortyn-code: The code, also called the Great Code, is known only from the inscription itself, cut on the circular wall of what may have been a bouleuterion or other public building in the agora of Gortyn. The building was 30 m in diameter; the twelve surviving columns of text are 10 m long and 1.5 m high and hold some 600 lines. It has been dated to the first half of the 5th century BCE.

It belongs to a tradition of Cretan law, the only substantial body of Greek law from antiquity found outside Athens. Earlier laws, of about 600 to 525 BCE, were inscribed on the steps and walls of the temple of Apollo Pythios, and the Great Code is one of a series written on walls in or near the agora between about 525 and 400 BCE.

The code distinguishes the free, the serf, the slave and the foreigner. Anyone bringing a suit is forbidden to seize the accused before trial, on pain of a fine that varies with the status of the person detained. Rape is punished by fines set largely by the difference in status between victim and accused. Adultery is treated similarly, with higher fines when it took place in the house of the woman's father, husband or brother; the fine falls on the man, and the code provides no punishment for the woman.

A divorced woman keeps the property she brought to the marriage and half of the income derived from it. A child conceived before a divorce and born after it belongs to the father and, if he does not accept it, to the mother. A widower holds his wife's property in trust and may not act on it without her children's consent; when a father dies, the land goes to the sons, and a childless widow is compelled to remarry. Adopted children inherit as natural children do, but women may not adopt.

The first fragment was discovered in 1857 by Georges Perrot and Louis Thenon. In 1884 the Italian archaeologist Federico Halbherr found four more columns while excavating near a local mill, and with Ernst Fabricius he uncovered eight further columns whose stones had been reused in the foundations of a Roman odeion of the 1st century BCE. The wall has since been partly reconstructed. All the Cretan legal texts are fragmentary and show continuous amendment, and from them scholars have traced the development of the law, notably the diminishing rights of women and the increasing rights of slaves.
gospel-of-john: The gospel is internally anonymous. It identifies an unnamed 'disciple whom Jesus loved' as its source and, perhaps, its author, a figure who appears at key episodes such as the Last Supper and the Empty Tomb. The traditional attribution to John the Apostle is first found in Irenaeus. Many modern scholars still affirm it, but most prefer alternatives such as John the Elder or Lazarus, while holding that the beloved disciple is the source of much of the content. Most critical commentaries consider that it was probably composed at Ephesus.

The gospel is usually divided into a prologue (1:1 to 1:18), an account of the ministry often called the Book of Signs (1:19 to 12:50), the final night, passion and resurrection (13:1 to 20:31) and an epilogue in chapter 21. The first part presents seven signs that culminate in the raising of Lazarus, and the second the Farewell Discourse and the passion and resurrection. The prologue identifies Jesus as the Logos, the Word, and calls the Word God; it contains some of the clearest identifications of Jesus with God in the New Testament.

It differs from the Synoptic Gospels. The ministry lasts three years, marked by three Passovers, and the cleansing of the Temple comes at its start. The death of Jesus is presented as his glorification and return to the Father, and he speaks of being lifted up. In place of the institution of the Eucharist, Jesus washes his disciples' feet. About 85 percent of its content is unique to it.

There is evidence that the gospel was circulating by the early second century: the First Epistle of John, which depends on it, was cited by Papias of Hierapolis. The attribution to John son of Zebedee was widespread by the mid-second century. Since the 19th century scholars have agreed that its long discourses are less likely to be historical than the Synoptic parables, though it is not without historical value, for example in its topographical references to Jerusalem and Judea. Early in the 20th century many scholars saw Gnostic elements in it, but most now consider the question closed. Augustine of Hippo and Thomas Aquinas wrote commentaries on it.
gospel-of-luke: Together with the Acts of the Apostles the Gospel of Luke forms a two-volume work called Luke–Acts, which makes up 27.5 per cent of the New Testament, the largest share by a single author. The text does not name its author. A church tradition first recorded by Irenaeus (c. 130 – c. 202 CE) identifies him as the Luke named as a companion of Paul in three of the Pauline letters. Most scholars hold that the author met Paul as a travelling companion, though some point to differences between Luke–Acts and the authentic letters of Paul.

Most scholars date the work to about 80–90 CE, since it knows the Gospel of Mark and the destruction of Jerusalem but not the Pauline letters. Mark supplied the narrative outline, and about 550 verses, nearly half the gospel, are found only in Luke. In his preface the author addresses Theophilus, whom most interpreters take to be a Christian convert and literary patron.

After the preface and the birth narratives of John the Baptist and of Jesus, the gospel opens in Galilee, where Jesus preaches the kingdom of God. It then moves to the journey to Jerusalem, its central section, and to the confrontation with the leaders of the Temple, the last supper, the arrest and crucifixion. It ends with the events from the first Easter to the Ascension, which anticipate Acts.

The gospel sets out a salvation history in three stages: the Law and the prophets, the time of Jesus, and the period of the church. The Holy Spirit has a greater part in it than in the other gospels and is the basis of the Christian community. Luke also holds that Christians are no threat to the Roman order.

No original copy of Luke survives. Early manuscripts fall into two families, the Alexandrian and the Western, and the dominant view is that the Western text results from a deliberate revision in the second century. The fragment 𝔓4 is often cited as the oldest, dated to the late second century, although the dating is disputed. Papyrus 75 includes an attribution of the gospel to Luke. The oldest complete texts are the 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae gives Luke in Greek and Latin on facing pages.
gothenburg: Gothenburg lies on the west coast of southwestern Sweden, about halfway between Copenhagen and Oslo, at the mouth of the Göta älv, which feeds into the Kattegat, an arm of the North Sea. Scandinavia's largest drainage basin enters the sea there, and the position has helped the city grow as a trading centre. The archipelago off the city consists of rough, barren rocks and cliffs, typical of the coast of Bohuslän. Because of the Gulf Stream the climate is mild, and warmer than that of places at a similar latitude such as Stockholm.

In the early modern period the shape of Sweden's borders made Gothenburg strategically critical. It was the only Swedish gateway to the Skagerrak, the North Sea and the Atlantic, on a very narrow strip of Swedish territory between Danish Halland in the south and Norwegian Bohuslän in the north. After several failed attempts, King Gustavus Adolphus founded it by royal charter in 1621 as a heavily fortified, primarily Dutch, trading colony. An earlier city founded in 1604 had burned down in 1611.

During the Thirty Years' War he gave generous privileges, such as tax relaxation, to his Dutch allies, and he also attracted German and Scottish allies to populate his only town on the western coast. The city council of 1641 had four Swedish, three Dutch, three German and two Scottish members.

The charter of 1621 named the city Göteborg, after the Göta älv and other cities ending in -borg, and gave it at the same time the German and English name Gothenburg. Its trading status was furthered by the founding of the Swedish East India Company. In the eighteenth century the Company made Gothenburg an important trade city, and imposing stone houses in Neo-Classical style were erected around the canals. In the nineteenth century the wealthy bourgeoisie moved outside the city walls, while the working class lived in wooden houses in the overcrowded district of Haga. Gothenburg became a city municipality with an elected council when the first Swedish local government acts were implemented in 1863.

Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden after Stockholm and the seat of Västra Götaland County. Its port is the largest in the Nordic countries, and trade, shipping and manufacturing have long been the pillars of its economy. Because all but the military and royal houses were built of wood, very few buildings survive from the seventeenth century; among them are Kronhuset, the Torstenson Palace and the fortresses Skansen Kronan and Skansen Lejonet. The East India House now holds the Göteborg City Museum, and the city is home to the University of Gothenburg and Chalmers University of Technology.
gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz: Gottfried Leibniz was born on 1 July 1646 in Leipzig, in the Electorate of Saxony, to Friedrich Leibniz and Catharina Schmuck. His father, a professor of moral philosophy at the University of Leipzig, died when he was six, and he inherited his father's library, to which he had free access from the age of seven. It let him read advanced philosophical and theological works he would not otherwise have met until college, and it led to his proficiency in Latin by the age of 12. At 13 he composed 300 hexameters of Latin verse in a single morning for a special event at school.

In mathematics Leibniz developed differential and integral calculus independently of Newton. Newton had developed his theory earlier, in 1666, but Leibniz's notation has been favoured as the conventional and more exact expression of calculus. He was the first to use the notion of a function explicitly, in 1692 and 1694, and he is credited with devising the modern binary number system, though the English astronomer Thomas Harriot had devised the same system decades before. In 1685 he was the first to describe a pinwheel calculator.

As a philosopher he dated his beginning to the Discourse on Metaphysics of 1686, and he published only two philosophical books in his lifetime, De Arte Combinatoria and the Théodicée of 1710. His optimism held that our world is, in a qualified sense, the best possible world that God could have created. Against Newton he argued that space, time and motion are relative, not absolute. In 1677 he called for a European confederation governed by a senate, and he noted that the hexagrams of the I Ching correspond to binary numbers.

Leibniz died on 14 November 1716, when his reputation was in decline. He was remembered for only one book, the Théodicée, whose argument Voltaire lampooned in Candide so influentially that many took the satire for an accurate description. His disciple Christian Wolff did him harm, and philosophical fashion was moving away from the rationalism of the 17th century. His reputation began to recover with the publication of his New Essays on Human Understanding in 1765. Only in 1895, when Bodemann completed a catalogue of his manuscripts, did the extent of his literary estate become clear: about 15,000 letters to more than 1,000 recipients and more than 40,000 other items.
granada: Granada lies in Andalusia at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, at the confluence of four rivers, the Darro, the Genil, the Monachil and the Beiro. It sits on the Vega de Granada, at an average elevation of 738 m and about 50 km from the Mediterranean coast. The pomegranate, granada in Spanish, is its heraldic device. The meaning of its Arabic name, Ġarnāṭa, is uncertain and debated.

The area has been populated since at least 5500 BCE. The oldest ruins belong to an oppidum called Ilturir, founded by the Iberian Bastetani around 650 BCE, later known as Iliberri or Iliberis, which became a Roman colony in 44 BCE. After the Umayyad conquest from 711 CE, the main settlement in the area was Madīnat Ilbīra (Elvira), while a smaller fortified settlement, Ġarnāṭa, with a mainly Jewish population, stood on the Albaicín site. Granada became a major city of al-Andalus in the 11th century under the Zirid Taifa of Granada.

As Almohad rule collapsed after 1228, Castile took Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248. Ibn al-Ahmar (Muhammad I) established the Nasrid dynasty, the last and longest reigning Muslim dynasty in the peninsula, ruling the Emirate of Granada. He became a vassal of Ferdinand III of Castile in 1246, and Granada thereafter was a tributary state of Castile, though wars often interrupted this. On 2 January 1492 Emir Muhammad XI, called Boabdil by the Spanish, surrendered the emirate to the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile. The city was progressively made a Christian city during the 16th century, and the University of Granada was founded in 1531 by Charles V.

Granada is the capital of the province of Granada, with a population of 233,532 in 2024. The Alhambra, a fortified palace complex on the Sabika hill and one of the best-preserved palaces of the historic Islamic world, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984. The Albaicín and other medieval monuments preserve Islamic-period influence, and the 16th century brought Mudéjar and Renaissance architecture. The Sacromonte, with cave houses dug into the hillside, has a reputation as a centre of flamenco.
graz: Graz lies on both sides of the river Mur in southeast Austria, about 150 kilometres southwest of Vienna and some 50 kilometres north of Maribor in Slovenia. It is in the Graz Basin on the eastern edge of the Alps, with the city centre at 353 metres, and the Schlossberg, or Castle Hill, 475 metres high, dominates the old town. Because the basin is open only to the south, the climate is warmer than expected at that latitude.

The oldest settlement on the site dates to the Copper Age, but there is no continuity of settlement before the Middle Ages. The name most likely derives from the Slavic gradec, small castle, though the city itself was founded by Bavarian settlers who arrived shortly after the Slavs and intermixed with them. They called it Bayrischgraz, Bavarian Graz, to distinguish it from the older Windischgraz, Slovenian Graz, which it soon eclipsed. The name first appears in records in 1128, and the earliest documented mention dates from the 12th century, when Graz developed as a fortified settlement under the Babenbergs.

In the Late Middle Ages Graz became a commercial and administrative centre and the residence of the Inner Austrian branch of the Habsburg dynasty, from which come many of its Renaissance and Baroque buildings. It was also a stronghold against the Ottoman Empire, through the fortifications on the Schlossberg. As capital of the multiethnic Duchy of Styria it was a centre of Slovene culture from the founding of the University of Graz in 1586 until the University of Ljubljana was established in 1919. Industrialisation in the 19th and 20th centuries made it a major industrial and cultural centre of southern Austria.

Graz is the capital of the Austrian state of Styria and the second-largest city in Austria after Vienna, with 307,912 residents with a primary residence. Its historic centre, with over 1,000 buildings from the Gothic to the contemporary, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1999, and Eggenberg Palace on the western edge of the city in 2010. Graz was European Capital of Culture in 2003, and the Clock Tower on the Schlossberg is its symbol.
