great-lakes: The Great Lakes are a series of interconnected freshwater lakes spanning the Canada-United States border: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario. Hydrologically, Michigan and Huron are a single body of water joined at the Straits of Mackinac. Water flows from Superior to Huron and Michigan, south to Erie and finally north to Lake Ontario, and leaves by the Saint Lawrence River to the Atlantic. The lakes hold more than 20 per cent of the world's surface fresh water, and because of their rolling waves and distant horizons they have long been called inland seas.
The lakes began to form at the end of the Last Glacial Period around 14,000 years ago, as retreating ice sheets exposed the basins they had carved and meltwater filled them.

Indigenous peoples, called Paleo-indians, inhabited the region around 10,000 BCE. From around 1000 CE the peoples of the region traded copper nuggets, which were fashioned into ornaments and weapons found in the mounds of southern Ohio. Several lake names come from Indigenous languages: Erie from an Iroquoian word for long tail, Michigan from the Ojibwe mishi-gami, great water, and Ontario from the Wendat ontarí'io, lake of shining waters. The first French explorers named Lake Huron for the Wendat.

After the War of 1812 the Rush-Bagot Treaty of 1818, and later the Treaty of Washington, eventually led to a complete disarmament of naval vessels on the lakes. Storms and reefs have sunk hundreds of ships, and the Lake Superior shipwreck coast from Grand Marais, Michigan, to Whitefish Point became known as the Graveyard of the Great Lakes.

The Great Lakes Waterway connects all five lakes, and the Saint Lawrence Seaway links them to the Atlantic. Most trade is in bulk goods such as iron ore, grain and potash, and large sections of the lakes freeze in winter. Major cities of the region include Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland, Buffalo and Milwaukee on the American side and Toronto, Mississauga and Hamilton on the Canadian side.
great-wall-of-china: The Chinese were already familiar with wall-building by the Spring and Autumn period, between the 8th and 5th centuries BCE. During that time and the Warring States period that followed, states such as Zheng, Chu, Qin, Wei, Zhao, Qi and Yan built extensive fortifications to defend their own borders. These were made mostly of stone or of earth and gravel stamped between board frames.

After Qin emerged victorious in 221 BCE, its ruler, the First Emperor, ordered the destruction of the wall sections that divided his empire among the former states. To position the empire against the Xiongnu, however, he had new walls built to connect the remaining fortifications along the northern frontier. The guiding principle was Build and move on, implying that the walls were not a permanently fixed border. Later the Han, the Northern dynasties and the Sui repaired, rebuilt or expanded sections at great cost, while the Tang and Song undertook no significant effort in the region.

The Ming dynasty made the most substantial contributions after its defeat by the Oirats at the Battle of Tumu. Dynasties founded by non-Han peoples, among them the Northern Wei, the Liao, the Jin and the Western Xia, also built walls, further north than the Han ones. A survey reported in 2012 concluded that the walls and trenches of all periods span 21,196.18 km, of which the Ming wall measures 8,850 km.

Before the Ming the wall was mainly rammed earth, stone and wood. The Ming used bricks heavily, which were easier to work with and bore more weight, and cut stone for foundations and gateways. Sticky rice mortar, made of sticky rice soup and slaked lime, held the bricks together. Signal towers on hilltops allowed units to call reinforcements and warn garrisons.

The name Long Wall appears in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian. Because of the wall's association with the First Emperor's supposed tyranny, later dynasties usually avoided that name for their own additions. Only in the Qing period did it become the general term. The belief that the wall can be seen from the Moon is a myth; an early reference to the claim is a letter of 1754 by the antiquary William Stukeley.
greece: Greece lies mostly on the Balkan peninsula, with thousands of islands, and has the longest coastline on the Mediterranean basin, 13,676 kilometres. It consists of a mountainous mainland that ends at the Peloponnese peninsula, which the canal of the Isthmus of Corinth separates from the mainland. About 80% of the country is mountains or hills. Mount Olympus, the mythical abode of the Greek gods ruled by Zeus, reaches 2,918 metres at Mytikas peak, and the Pindus range has historically been a significant barrier to east–west travel. Extensive plains lie in Thessaly, Central Macedonia and Thrace, and are among the few arable places.

Neolithic settlements in Greece, dating from the 7th millennium BCE, are the oldest in Europe. The Cycladic culture flourished on the Aegean islands from around 3200 BCE, and from c. 3100 BCE to 1100 BCE Crete was home to the Minoan civilisation, which wrote in the undeciphered scripts Linear A and Cretan hieroglyphs. On the mainland the Mycenaean civilisation developed around 1750 BCE and lasted until c. 1100 BCE.

Its people used Linear B to write the earliest attested form of Greek. After its collapse came the Greek Dark Ages, from which written records are absent, traditionally ended in 776 BCE, the year of the first Olympic Games. Many kingdoms and city-states emerged, and some founded colonies in Asia Minor, on the Black Sea shores and in southern Italy. In 508 BCE Cleisthenes instituted the first democratic system of government in Athens.

Philip II of Macedon united most of present-day Greece in the fourth century BCE, and the Hellenistic period followed his son Alexander the Great's conquests. Rome annexed Greece in the second century BCE, and it remained part of the Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire. After the Fourth Crusade in 1204 Greek lands fragmented into Latin and Byzantine successor states, and most came under Ottoman control by the mid-15th century. A war of independence from 1821 produced a modern nation state in 1830. The Kingdom of Greece expanded in the Balkan Wars (1912–1913) and the First World War until its defeat in the Greco-Turkish War in 1922.

Greece endured military occupation in the Second World War, then the Greek Civil War and a military dictatorship from 1967 to 1974. The present constitution, enacted in 1975, makes it a parliamentary republic with a 300-member unicameral Parliament. Greece joined what is now the European Union in 1981 and adopted the euro in January 2001. The population was estimated at 10.6 million in 2022, and Athens and Thessaloniki are the two largest cities.
greek-language: Greek has been spoken in the Balkan peninsula since around the 3rd millennium BCE, or possibly earlier. The earliest written evidence is a Linear B clay tablet found in Messenia, dating to between 1450 and 1350 BCE, which makes Greek the oldest recorded living language. Proto-Greek, the assumed last common ancestor, is unrecorded. Greek forms an independent branch of the Indo-European family, and current consensus regards the extinct Phrygian language as its closest relative.

The language is conventionally divided into Mycenaean Greek, recorded in Linear B from the 15th century BCE; Ancient Greek, in its various dialects; and later Koine, Medieval and Modern Greek. Such divisions are relatively arbitrary, since Ancient Greek has enjoyed high prestige in every period. The dative case fell out of use, and the pitch accent was replaced by a stress accent during the Hellenistic and Roman period.

Linear B, a syllabary, was the first script used for Greek and was deciphered in the 1950s by Michael Ventris and John Chadwick, building on the research of Alice Kober. The Greek alphabet has been in use since about the 9th century BCE and was made by modifying the Phoenician alphabet, with the innovation of letters for vowels.

During antiquity Greek was by far the most widely spoken lingua franca of the Mediterranean world, and it eventually became the official language of the Byzantine Empire. It fell into disuse in Western Europe in the Middle Ages and was reintroduced after the fall of Constantinople. It was also the language of government and religion in the Christian Nubian kingdoms for most of their history. Homer's epic poetry begins a literature of lasting importance, many foundational texts of science and philosophy were composed in Greek, and the New Testament was originally written in it. Words such as mathematics, democracy, philosophy and theatre are of Greek origin.
greenland: Greenland is the world's largest non-continental island, lying between latitudes 59° and 83°N, with over 80% of its land north of the Arctic Circle. Its area is 2,166,086 square kilometres, of which the ice sheet covers about 81%. The highest point is Gunnbjørn Fjeld, at 3,700 metres, but most of the island lies below 1,500 metres. Nearly all of its people live along the fjords of the south-west, where the climate is relatively mild.

The early Norse settlers gave the island its name. The sagas say that Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, named the land Grœnland in the hope that a pleasant name would attract settlers. In the Greenlandic language it is Kalaallit Nunaat, land of the Kalaallit, the principal group of Greenlandic Inuit in the west.

Successive Palaeo-Inuit cultures, known mainly from archaeology, lived on the island. The first entry is thought to have been about 2500 BCE. The Saqqaq culture inhabited the south and west from about 2500 to 800 BCE, with most finds around Disko Bay, and the Independence I culture lived in the north from 2400 to 1300 BCE. About 800 BCE the Saqqaq culture disappeared, and the Early Dorset and Independence II cultures emerged. The Thule people entered later from the north.

From the late 10th century Icelanders and Norwegians settled the west coast, in a contingent of 14 boats led by Erik the Red. They formed the Eastern, Western and Middle Settlements on fjords near the south-western tip. The Norse Greenlanders submitted to the Kingdom of Norway in 1261. Settlements such as Brattahlíð lasted for centuries but vanished in the 15th century, perhaps at the onset of the Little Ice Age. Dano-Norwegian explorers returned in the 17th century, found the earlier settlement extinct and re-established a Scandinavian presence.

Greenland passed from the Norwegian to the Danish crown when Denmark and Norway separated in 1814. Denmark integrated it into the Danish Realm in 1952, ending its colonial status, and granted home rule in 1979. The Self-Government Act, passed after a referendum in 2008, transferred further areas of government to the Naalakkersuisut, the Greenlandic government, and made Greenlandic the sole official language in 2009.

Greenland is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, with Nuuk as its capital and largest city. A population of 56,583 was counted in 2022, most of them Greenlandic Inuit, with a Danish minority. Its parliament is the Inatsisartut. Greenlandic culture blends Inuit and Scandinavian traditions, among them the carved ivory figures called tupilak.
grenoble: Grenoble lies where the river Drac flows into the Isère at the foot of the French Alps. It is surrounded by mountains, with the Chartreuse to the north, the Vercors to the south and west and the Belledonne range to the east, and it is regarded as the capital of the French Alps. The Bastille, a series of fortifications on the mountainside, overlooks the city from the north. It was begun in the Middle Ages and extended in later centuries, and it has been credited as the most extensive example of early 18th-century fortification in France, on what was then the Alpine frontier with the Kingdom of Sardinia.

The first references to the place date to 43 BCE, when Cularo was a village of the Allobroges, a Gallic tribe, near a bridge over the Isère. The Emperor Gratian visited it and made it a Roman city, and in 381 it was renamed Gratianopolis, the city of Gratian, which through regular sound shifts became Graignovol in the Middle Ages and then Grenoble.

After the fall of the Roman Empire the city became part of the first Burgundian kingdom in the 5th century and then of the Kingdom of Burgundy until 1032, when it was integrated into the Holy Roman Empire. Grenoble grew significantly in the 11th century, when the Counts of Albon chose it as the capital of their scattered territories, and when they took the title of Dauphins it became the capital of the State of Dauphiné. The Parlement of Dauphiné sat in a Renaissance palace built around 1500 until the French Revolution.

The revocation of the Edict of Nantes by Louis XIV caused 2,000 Protestants to leave Grenoble, which weakened the economy but also the glove industry of Grasse, and so left Grenoble's glove makers without competition. At the start of the 18th century 12 glovers made 180,000 gloves a year, and by 1787 there were 64 making 1,920,000.

Grenoble is the prefecture and largest city of the Isère department in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region. The commune had 156,140 inhabitants in 2023 and its metropolitan area 727,380, the largest in the Alps. It is a significant European scientific centre, and its post-war boom was symbolised by the Olympic Winter Games of 1968.
gross-domestic-product: Sir William Petty devised a concept of gross domestic product to calculate the tax burden, and to argue that landlords were unfairly taxed during the warfare between the Dutch and the English between 1652 and 1674. Charles Davenant developed the method further in 1695. The economist Simon Kuznets, who developed the first comprehensive set of measures of national income, warned of the uses and abuses of such measurements in his second report to the United States Congress in 1937. The international standard for measuring GDP is the System of National Accounts, prepared by representatives of the International Monetary Fund, the European Union, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the United Nations and the World Bank.

Gross domestic product is the total market value of all final goods and services produced during a specific period, usually a year, by a country or countries. It can be determined in three ways that should in theory give the same result: the production approach, which sums the value added at each stage of production, the income approach, which adds the incomes paid to the factors of production, and the expenditure approach, which sums consumption, investment, government expenditure and net exports. Nominal GDP does not account for inflation, so comparisons over time use real values, and comparisons between countries are often adjusted for differences in the cost of living. GDP defines its scope by location, whereas gross national income defines it by ownership.

GDP is widely used as a broad measure of economic progress, but it has been criticised for leaving out externalities such as environmental harm, unpaid domestic work, non-market transactions and economies where little money is used. It also does not account for how income is distributed. In the 1980s Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum developed the capability approach, which looks at what people are able to achieve rather than at aggregate output. A commission including Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen and Jean-Paul Fitoussi proposed in 2009 a well-being framework to broaden the focus beyond GDP.
grover-cleveland: Stephen Grover Cleveland was born on 18 March 1837 in Caldwell, New Jersey, the son of Richard Falley Cleveland, a Congregational and Presbyterian minister, and Ann Neal. After his father died in 1853 he left school to help support his family, and in 1855 he decided to move west. He started his own law practice in 1862, and in January 1863 he became assistant district attorney of Erie County, New York. A Democrat from the start, he was elected mayor of Buffalo in 1881, on a ticket meant to attract voters tired of corrupt party machines, and governor of New York in 1882.

In 1884 reform-minded Republicans called Mugwumps denounced the Republican nominee, James G. Blaine, as corrupt and supported Cleveland, whose slogan was 'A public office is a public trust'. As president he said he would not dismiss Republicans who did their work well, and he vetoed hundreds of private pension bills for Civil War veterans, 414 vetoes in his first term, more than four times as many as any earlier president.

He signed the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 and the Dawes Act, which led Native Americans to cede about 100 million acres between 1887 and 1934. On 2 June 1886 he married Frances Folsom in the White House, the only president to marry there. In 1888 he won the popular vote but lost the electoral college to Benjamin Harrison.

He defeated Harrison in 1892. The Panic of 1893 struck shortly before his second term, and he persuaded Congress to repeal the silver coinage provisions of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, which alienated the agrarian wing of his party. In 1894 the Pullman Strike put 125,000 railroad workers on strike; Cleveland obtained an injunction and sent federal troops into Chicago and 20 other rail centres, and the use of troops hardened organised labour against him. An anti-imperialist, he opposed the annexation of Hawaii and investigated the 1893 coup against Queen Liliʻuokalani. By the end of his second term he was highly unpopular, even among Democrats.

After leaving the White House, Cleveland served as a trustee of Princeton University. He joined the American Anti-Imperialist League in protest at the Spanish-American War of 1898, and he died on 24 June 1908. He was the first Democrat elected president after the Civil War and the first president to serve non-consecutive terms.
guangzhou: Guangzhou lies on the Pearl River in south-central Guangdong, about 120 km northwest of Hong Kong and 145 km north of Macau. The old town stood near Baiyun Mountain on the east bank, about 130 km from the river's junction with the South China Sea, and commanded the alluvial plain of the Pearl River Delta, with its link to the sea guarded at the Humen Strait. The city name comes from the ancient Guang Prefecture, whose seat it became.

Before the Han conquest the area was inhabited by non-Chinese tribes known collectively as the Baiyue. A settlement now called Nanwucheng was present by 1100 BCE, and some traditional Chinese histories place its founding in the reign of King Nan of Zhou. Under the name Panyu the city was founded on the east bank of the Pearl River in 214 BCE. Incorporated into the Han dynasty, Panyu became a provincial capital, and in 226 CE it became the seat of Guang Prefecture, which gave it its modern name. The Old Book of Tang describes it as an important port.

Relations with foreign traders were sometimes violent. Arab and Persian pirates sacked the city on 30 October 758, during the An Lushan Rebellion. In 878 the rebel Huang Chao killed about 200,000 foreigners there, along with the city's Jews, Christians and Parsis, and the port was closed for fifty years. For a long time Guangzhou was the only Chinese port accessible to Europeans. It was captured by the British in the First Opium War and lost its monopoly, though it remained a major entrepôt. In the late Qing period it was the site of the revolutionary uprisings of 1895 and 1911.

Guangzhou, also called Canton, is the capital and largest city of Guangdong and a major port and transport hub. The 2020 census recorded a registered population of 18,676,605. Cantonese culture, including Cantonese cuisine and Cantonese opera, is its main cultural heritage. The Canton Fair, formally the China Import and Export Fair, was inaugurated in the spring of 1957 and is held each April and October. Its metro, the fourth underground railway in mainland China, opened in 1997.
guatemala: Guatemala is mountainous. Two mountain chains enter it from west to east and divide it into three regions: the highlands, the Pacific coast to the south and the Petén region, a sparsely populated northern lowland. All major cities lie in the highlands and on the Pacific coast. The highlands lie along the Motagua Fault, which produced a 7.5 magnitude earthquake on 4 February 1976 that killed more than 25,000 people. Two of the three moves of the capital were caused by volcanic mudflows in 1541 and earthquakes in 1773.

The first evidence of human habitation dates to 12,000 BCE, and maize cultivation had been developed by 3500 BCE. Archaeologists divide the pre-Columbian past into the Preclassic period (2000 BCE to 250 CE), the Classic (250 to 900) and the Postclassic (900 to 1500). The Classic period matches the height of Maya civilisation, with the largest concentration of sites in Petén. That civilisation collapsed around 900 and many cities of the central lowlands were abandoned; the cause is debated, though the drought theory is gaining currency. In the Postclassic, regional kingdoms such as the Itza and Kowoj in Petén and the K'iche', Kaqchikel and Mam peoples in the highlands preserved many aspects of Maya culture.

Most of the territory was conquered by the Spanish in the 16th century and claimed as part of the viceroyalty of New Spain. Guatemala became independent from Spain and Mexico in 1821 and was part of the Federal Republic of Central America from 1823 to 1841. Jorge Ubico was overthrown in 1944, beginning a decade of reform that ended with a military coup in 1954. A civil war ran from 1960 to 1996 and included genocidal massacres of the Maya population by the military; 83 percent of the victims of the 626 massacres reported in the 1980s were Maya. A peace accord negotiated by the United Nations ended it.

Guatemala is a constitutional democratic republic with its capital and largest city at Guatemala City. The sole official language is Spanish, and twenty-one Mayan languages, Xinca and Garifuna are recognised as national languages. Indigenous Guatemalans, mostly Maya, are 43.6% of the population according to the 2018 census. The country is divided into 22 departments.
guatemala-city: Guatemala City lies in a mountain valley called the Valle de la Ermita, in the south-central part of Guatemala. Four stratovolcanoes are visible from the city, two of them active, and the nearest and most active, Pacaya, at times sends up a considerable amount of ash. The Guatemalan highlands lie on the Ring of Fire and are frequently shaken by earthquakes; the last large one to strike the region came in 1976, on the Motagua Fault.

Human settlement on the site began with the Maya, who built a large ceremonial centre at Kaminaljuyu. It was the biggest Maya settlement outside the lowlands of the Yucatán Peninsula and rose to prominence about 300 BCE through the mining and trade of obsidian, a volcanic glass valued across Mesoamerica. The centre is now a park within the city.

The old colonial capital, now Antigua Guatemala, was left in ruins by the earthquakes of 1773, the third to strike it after those of 1717 and 1751, and the Spanish decided to move to a safer place. In 1776 the capital was moved to the valley where Guatemala City stands. The Metropolitan Cathedral on the central plaza was built mostly between 1782 and 1815 and completed in 1871. The Act of Independence of Central America, declared in the city in September 1821, ended Spanish rule, and for several decades the city was the capital of the federation of the United Provinces of Central America. In August 1847 Guatemala declared itself an independent republic and Guatemala City became its national capital.

The earthquakes of 1917 and 1918 almost completely destroyed the city, and its reconstruction brought wider streets and grid layouts. Under President Jorge Ubico, who held power for 13 years, the National Palace was built between 1939 and 1943. He was overthrown in the Guatemalan Revolution of 1944.

Guatemala City is the national capital and largest city of Guatemala, and its metropolitan area is the largest in Central America. Its formal name is Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción, in honour of the Virgin of the Assumption, whose feast on 15 August is the city's feast day. The University of San Carlos of Guatemala, founded in 1676, is the oldest institution of higher education in Central America.
guinea: Guinea is a coastal country in West Africa, roughly the size of the United Kingdom, with 320 kilometres of coastline. It forms a crescent curving from the southeast to the north and west. It is divided into four regions: Maritime Guinea on the Atlantic coast, populated mainly by the Susu; the cooler, mountainous Fouta Djallon in the middle, populated by the Fula; Upper Guinea, a Sahelian region in the northeast, populated by the Malinké; and the forested southeast with several ethnic groups. The Guinea Highlands are the source of the Niger, the Gambia and the Senegal rivers, and the highest point is Mount Nimba at 1,752 metres.

The country is named after the Guinea region along the Gulf of Guinea. The English term comes from the Portuguese word Guiné, which emerged in the mid-15th century for the lands of the Guineus, a generic term for the African peoples south of the Senegal River. In 1978 the official name became the People's Revolutionary Republic of Guinea, and in 1984, after the death of the first president, Ahmed Sékou Touré, it was renamed the Republic of Guinea.

What is now Guinea sat on the fringes of various West African empires. The Ghana Empire grew on trade and fell after repeated incursions by the Almoravids, and Islam first arrived in the region in this period through North African traders. The Sosso Empire held the area in the 12th and 13th centuries. The Mali Empire followed after Soundiata Kéïta defeated the Sosso ruler Soumangourou Kanté at the Battle of Kirina, c. 1235. Its rulers included Kankou Moussa, who made a hajj to Mecca in 1324. After his reign it declined and was supplanted by its vassal states in the 15th century.

The Songhai Empire expanded its power from about 1460 and fell to invaders from Morocco in 1591. Fulani Muslims migrated to Futa Jallon in central Guinea and established an Islamic state from 1727 to 1896, with a written constitution and alternating rulers. The Wassoulou Empire, led by Samori Toure from 1878 to 1898 in the Malinké area of upper Guinea and southwestern Mali, moved to Ivory Coast before the French occupied it. France claimed the territory in the 1890s as part of French West Africa, and Guinea declared independence on 2 October 1958.

Guinea is the Republic of Guinea, with its capital and largest city at Conakry. French is the language of schools and administration, and more than 24 indigenous languages are spoken, the largest being Susu, Pular and Maninka. Most of the population is Muslim. Guinea has large reserves of bauxite, and the Nimba Massif is a UNESCO strict nature reserve on the Guinean and Ivorian sides.
guinea-bissau: Guinea-Bissau lies on the West African coast, bordered by Senegal to the north, Guinea to the south and east and the Atlantic Ocean to the west. Its area of 36,125 square kilometres is larger than Belgium's. The terrain is mostly low coastal plains with Guinean mangrove swamps, rising to a forest and savannah mosaic in the east, and the highest point is Monte Torin at 262 metres. The Bijagós Archipelago of 88 islands and islets lies off the mainland. A rainy season from June to September or October alternates with a dry season, and from December through April the country experiences drought.

The ancient history of the area is poorly understood. The earliest inhabitants were the Jola, Papel, Manjak, Balanta and Biafada peoples, and the Mandinka and Fulani migrated into the region in the 13th and 15th centuries, pushing the earlier inhabitants toward the coast and onto the Bijagós islands. The Balanta and Jola had weak or non-existent kingship and placed power in the heads of villages and families, whereas the chiefs of the Mandinka, Fula, Papel, Manjak and Biafada were vassals to kings. Trade was widespread between groups in pepper and kola nuts, iron utensils, salt and dried fish, and Mandinka cotton cloth.

The Biafada lived in three kingdoms, Biguba, Guinala and Bissege, and were subjects of the Mandinka mansa of Kaabu. According to oral tradition the Kingdom of Bissau was founded by a son of the king of Quinara. It defended its sovereignty against Portuguese 'Pacification Campaigns', defeating them in 1891, 1894 and 1904, but was fully absorbed in 1915 by the Portuguese under Officer Teixeira Pinto and the warlord Abdul Injai. On the Bijagós Islands, Bijago society was warlike: men built boats and raided the mainland and other islands, while women cultivated the land and built houses.

Guinea-Bissau is the Republic of Guinea-Bissau. Its capital, Bissau, was added to its name after independence, declared in 1973 and recognised in 1974, to prevent confusion with Guinea. Portuguese is the official language, and Guinea-Bissau Creole is the national language. The music most associated with the country is the polyrhythmic gumbe, and the film director Flora Gomes made Mortu Nega in 1988, the first fiction film made there.
gujarat: Gujarat lies along the western coast of India and has the longest coastline of any Indian state, most of it on the Kathiawar peninsula. It borders Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and the Arabian Sea, and on the northwest the Pakistani province of Sindh, from which the Rann of Kutch, a seasonally marshy saline clay desert, separates it. Historically the north was known as Anarta, the Kathiawar peninsula as Saurastra and the south as Lata. The name is generally believed to derive from the Gurjars: parts of modern Rajasthan and Gujarat were known as the Gurjarat region for centuries before the Mughal period.

Gujarat was one of the central areas of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and about fifty settlements of that civilisation have been found there, among them Lothal, believed to have been one of the first seaports, Dholavira, one of the largest archaeological sites in India, and Gola Dhoro. Coastal cities, chiefly Bharuch and Khambhat, were ports and trading centres under the Maurya and Gupta empires and the Saka dynasties of the Western Satraps. In the early 8th century the Arabs of the Umayyad Caliphate tried to expand southeast from Sindh; campaigns fought in 730 ended in their defeat, probably by a coalition of Indian rulers.

Qutbuddin Aibak tried and failed to annex Gujarat in 1197. From 1297 to 1300 Alauddin Khalji, Sultan of Delhi, destroyed the city of Anhilwara and brought it into the Delhi Sultanate. After Timur sacked Delhi, the governor Zafar Khan Muzaffar asserted independence, and his son Sultan Ahmed Shah (ruled 1411 to 1442) made Ahmedabad the capital. In 1664 and again in 1672 the Maratha ruler Shivaji attacked Surat. By then the Portuguese, followed by the Dutch and English, had bases on the coast; after the Battle of Diu the Portuguese held enclaves including Daman and Diu until India took them on 19 December 1961.

Gujarat is a state of India with its capital at Gandhinagar, a planned city, and its largest city at Ahmedabad. Gujarati is the official language, and the 2011 census counted 60,439,692 people. Its tradition of seafaring and long-distance trade carried Gujarati merchants to the Persian Gulf, the Horn of Africa and Indonesia. Somnath, the Sun Temple at Modhera, the Jain pilgrimage mountain of Shatrunjaya at Palitana and the Gir forest, the only home of wild Asiatic lions, are among its lasting sites, and Mahatma Gandhi was born at Porbandar.
gustav-mahler: Mahler was born on 7 July 1860 in the village of Kaliště in Bohemia, the second son of a German-speaking Jewish family of humble circumstances. His father, Bernhard Mahler, rose from a pedlar's family to become a coachman and then an innkeeper, and married Marie Herrmann in 1857. They had 14 children. In December 1860 the family moved to Jihlava, where Bernhard built up a distillery and tavern business and where Gustav heard street songs, dance tunes, folk melodies and the trumpet calls of the local military band. These sounds later fed his musical vocabulary. He studied at the Vienna Conservatory from 1875 to 1878.

Mahler's first professional conducting job, in the summer of 1880, was an operetta season at the spa town of Bad Hall. Posts followed at Laibach, Prague, Leipzig, Budapest and Hamburg, each larger than the last. In Leipzig he took charge of most of Wagner's Ring cycle when a senior colleague fell ill, and scored a public success, though the orchestra resented his dictatorial manner and heavy rehearsals. In 1897 he became director of the Vienna Court Opera, having converted to Catholicism to secure the post. He also led the Vienna Philharmonic's subscription concerts from 1898 to 1901, and the anti-Semitic press attacked him throughout his ten years in the city.

Mahler made his New York debut at the Metropolitan Opera on 1 January 1908, conducting Wagner's Tristan und Isolde, and later led the New York Philharmonic. He gave his last concert at Carnegie Hall on 21 February 1911 with a fever. Diagnosed with bacterial endocarditis, he was taken back to Europe and died in a Vienna sanatorium on 18 May 1911, aged 50.

Composing was for most of his life a part-time activity, done in summer studios while conducting paid his living. Apart from juvenilia he wrote only songs and symphonies, and the two forms are closely linked: melodies of the song cycle Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen appear in the First Symphony, and Wunderhorn songs form movements of the Second, Third and Fourth. He told Sibelius that the symphony must be like the world and embrace everything, and his music mixes bird calls, bugle fanfares and street tunes with solemn matter. He left Das Lied von der Erde unnumbered, hoping to escape the curse of the Ninth Symphony.

His symphonies were often controversial when first performed. By his death there had been more than 260 performances of them. Nazi-era bans kept the music from much of Europe, but after 1945 a new generation rediscovered it. Arnold Schoenberg, Alban Berg and Anton Webern of the Second Viennese School were among his early admirers. The International Gustav Mahler Society was founded in 1955.
gustave-flaubert: Gustave Flaubert was born in Rouen on 12 December 1821, the second son of Anne Justine Caroline Fleuriot and Achille-Cléophas Flaubert, director and senior surgeon of the major hospital in Rouen. He began writing at an early age, as early as eight according to some sources. He was educated at the Lycée Pierre-Corneille and in 1840 went to Paris to study law, where he was an indifferent student and found the city distasteful. In 1846, after an attack of epilepsy, he left Paris and abandoned the study of law. He then returned to Croisset, near the Seine and close to Rouen, and lived there for the rest of his life.

His first finished work was a novella, November, completed in 1842. In September 1849 he completed the first version of The Temptation of Saint Anthony and read it aloud to Louis Bouilhet and Maxime Du Camp over four days. They told him to throw the manuscript in the fire and to write about day-to-day life instead. After returning from Egypt in 1850 he began Madame Bovary, which took five years to write and was serialised in the Revue de Paris in 1856. The government brought an action against publisher and author on a charge of immorality, but both were acquitted in 1857, and the book was warmly received.

In 1858 he travelled to Carthage to gather material for Salammbô, completed in 1862. Sentimental Education, published in 1869 after seven years, was his last complete novel; it follows a young man, Frédéric Moreau, through the Revolution of 1848 and the founding of the Second French Empire. Between 1875 and 1877 he wrote Three Tales, and he spent the rest of his life on the unfinished satire Bouvard et Pécuchet, published after his death in 1881. He was a prolific letter writer, and his Correspondence is among the works for which he is best known.

Flaubert pursued the principle of le mot juste, the right word, and avoided the inexact, the abstract and the cliché. He worked in solitude, sometimes spending a week on one page, and wrote that he wished to forge a style rhythmic as verse and precise as the language of the sciences.

He published far less than peers such as Balzac or Zola, and Walter Pater called him the martyr of style. Madame Bovary was followed by more scandal than admiration at first, but its scrupulously truthful portraiture of life was gradually accepted, and at his death he was widely regarded as the most influential French Realist. Guy de Maupassant, Émile Zola and Alphonse Daudet were among those he influenced. He died at Croisset of a cerebral haemorrhage on 8 May 1880, aged 58, and was buried in the family vault at Rouen.
